title: Percent vs. Percentage Points
objective: After this level you can tell a rise of 5 percentage points from a rise of 5 percent, and spot a headline that mixes them up.
summary: Going from 10% to 15% is a rise of 5 percentage points (subtract) and a 50 percent increase (divide by the start). Both are true; headlines often mix them up.

cards.headline: A share goes from 10% to 15%. Did it rise by 5 or by 50?
cards.body: Both answers are right, in different units. One counts percentage points; the other is a percent increase. Mix them up and a headline can make a change look far bigger or smaller than it is.

cards.headline: Points: just subtract
cards.body: When you compare two percentages, the plain difference is measured in percentage points. Say the share of students who walk to school goes from 10% to 15%. Subtract: 15 minus 10 is 5 percentage points. Points tell you how far the number moved on the scale from 0 to 100.

cards.headline: Percent: compare with the start
cards.body: Percent change uses Level 3's rule: change ÷ start. The change is 5 and the start is 10, and 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5, a 50% rise. Walkers really did grow by half: 10 in every 100 students became 15 in every 100. Both statements are true. They answer different questions.

mascot.line: People mix these two up all the time. Points: subtract. Percent: divide by the start.

cards.fact: "Percentage change and percentage-point change get mixed up all the time."
cards.context: That warning comes from Jennifer LaFleur, an editor quoted by The Journalist's Resource. The rule of thumb: when you compare two percentages, the difference is in percentage points. So a headline saying walkers are "up 5%" when the share went from 10% to 15% has undersold a 50% jump.

cards.headline: Points vs. percent: sorted
learned: Percent change: divide by the start
10% to 15% is 5 points and a 50% rise

questions.prompt: A share that rises from 10% to 15% has gone up by _____ percentage points.

options.rationale: That's the new share, not the difference.
50 is the percent increase, not the point difference.

questions.explanation: Percentage points are the plain difference: 15 minus 10 is 5 points.

questions.prompt: The same rise, from 10% to 15%, is also a 50 percent increase. Why?

options.label: The change of 5 is half of the starting 10
15 is 50 more than 10 on the 0 to 100 scale
options.rationale: On that scale it moved 5 points, not 50.

options.label: Percents always double when they rise
options.rationale: Nothing doubles here; the share grew by half.

options.label: Half of all students now walk
options.rationale: Only 15% walk; the growth, not the share, is 50%.

questions.explanation: Percent change divides the change by the start: 5 ÷ 10 = 0.5, a 50% increase.

questions.prompt: A share falls from 40% to 30%. Which headline describes it correctly?

options.label: "Down 10 percent"
options.rationale: It fell 10 points; as a percent change that is 10 ÷ 40, a 25% fall.

options.label: "Down 75 percent"
options.rationale: 30 is 75% of 40; the fall is 25%, or 10 points.

questions.explanation: Subtract the two percentages: 40 minus 30 is 10 percentage points (which is a 25% fall, by Level 3's rule).
